# Lottie animations

Played by `lottie-react-native`, which is a **native module** — adding or
upgrading the _package_ needs `npm run prebuild` and a fresh `npm run ios` /
`npm run android`. Adding a _file_ does not: these are ordinary `require`d JSON
and Metro bundles them, so a reload picks one up. A stale one usually means the
Metro cache, cleared with `npm start -- --clear`.

**Every file here is generated by a script in `script/`, and none was drawn by
hand.** That is not a stopgap. This project has no After Effects pipeline and no
artist, and a committed binary nobody can regenerate drifts from the palette the
moment a colour moves — the same argument the app icons and the splash are built
on. Shared primitives live in `script/lottie_kit.py`; each generator holds only
what is a choice, which is the frame, the timing, the palette entries that suit
that mark, and the shapes.

**Do not delete a generator and keep its JSON.** The pair is the source; the JSON
alone is a binary with no provenance.

## Files

| File            | Where it plays                      | Built by               |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `win.json`      | The win card, and the reward dialog | `make-lottie.py`       |
| `coins.json`    | The win card's coin shower          | `make-coins.py`        |
| `brew.json`     | Rewards' countdown, while it waits  | `make-brew.py`         |
| `loader.json`   | `AdVeil`, while a rewarded ad loads | `make-loader.py`       |
| `shine.json`    | The coin pill's plus                | `make-shine.py`        |
| `gift.json`     | Home's daily reward chip            | `make-gift.py`         |
| `advert.json`   | Home's rewarded-ad chip             | `make-advert.py`       |
| `tap.json`      | Press burst, on dark buttons        | Hand-written, stand-in |
| `tap-dark.json` | The same, on lit gold faces         | Hand-written, stand-in |

`brew.json`'s frame is 110x200 rather than square, so whatever box it is given must carry that
aspect — `contain` fits a tall frame into a square one by its width, which is
how it first shipped 18dp tall.

`loader.json` is generated by `python3 script/make-loader.py` — two gold arcs
turning against each other on a dim track, with a lit bead riding the head of the
outer one. Square frame, 120x120.

It went through three vials filling in turn first, on the reasoning that a loader
should speak the game's own vocabulary. On screen that was far too much: a wide
row of glassware doing a full pour-and-drain cycle, for a wait usually over in a
second. A loader is chrome. The theme is carried by the palette and the motion,
not by the object.

**No trim paths in it**, though a spinner is where one belongs. Trim's behaviour
depends on where the modifier sits in the group's item list, and the three
renderers resolve that differently — a hand-written one is a coin toss on whether
the arc draws at all. The arcs are plain bezier paths with the sweep baked in.

`shine.json` is generated by `python3 script/make-shine.py` — a wide specular
band with a narrow one trailing it, crossing a 60x60 frame once every 1.8 seconds
and parked outside it the rest of the time. The pause is the parking, not an
opacity fade.

**Tune it against the size it renders at.** It first shipped as a half-second
sweep every three seconds and was invisible on a device — not wrong, just
unnoticeable, because a 20dp disc in a corner gets a fraction of a second of
attention and the odds of that landing in a one-in-six window are poor.

**It is not masked and does not need to be.** `styles.plus` already carries
`borderRadius` and `overflow: 'hidden'` for its own gradient, so the disc clips
the band. That is what keeps the file inside the portable subset; see the trim
note above for what happens when you rely on the renderers agreeing.

`win.json` draws 46 confetti on ballistic arcs plus a gold ring pushing out of the centre, in the
palette's own colours.

It replaced a hand-written stand-in — three gold dots that expanded and faded —
which existed so the integration compiled, not because it looked like anything.
On a device the reward dialog read as a plain modal, because it was one.

Its seed is fixed, so a rerun is byte-identical and a regenerated file is not a
diff nobody can review. Confetti is also the one celebration shape that survives
being generated — many simple pieces under one physical rule, so it is
arithmetic rather than draughtsmanship. A drawn flourish would still need a
hand, and a real export can still be dropped over this.

## Before you commit a downloaded file

**Check its licence individually.** LottieFiles' free section mixes several:

- **Lottie Simple License** — commercial use, no attribution. What you want.
- **CC-BY** — usable, but you owe a credit somewhere in the app.
- **Preview only** — part of a paid pack. Not usable.

The licence is on each animation's own page, not on the site as a whole. This
is the same trap the audio work fell into: "free to download" is not "free to
ship".

## Fitting one to this app

Most free confetti and star animations are bright flat cartoon drawn for a white
background. This app is deep purple and gold, so a file that looks superb in the
preview can land on the win card looking borrowed.

Two things help:

- Prefer animations that are mostly white or monochrome. `LottieView` takes a
  `colorFilters` prop, so a single-colour animation can be tinted from
  `src/theme/colors.ts` rather than fighting the palette.
- Judge it on the card, not in the preview. The scrim, the gold buttons and the
  panel gloss are all competing for the same attention.

## Keep them one-shot

`loop={false}`. A looping animation on a mounted screen redraws forever, which
is the cost this project has already paid once on Home's rack — see the
`createPicture` note in `AGENTS.md`.

Two exemptions, each with its own argument, and a third loop needs one too.

`loader.json` earns it by being mounted only while an ad is being fetched —
`AdVeil` unmounts the instant the fetch ends. A loader that plays once and stops
is worse than none, because a frozen spinner says the app has hung.

`shine.json` earns it by being 20dp. It is mounted for as long as the coin pill
is, which is most of the app, so the redraw is permanent — but it is confined to
400 square points, and five sixths of its cycle is a band parked outside the
frame with nothing changing. At any larger size the answer would be no.

`gift.json`, `advert.json`, `arrow.json` and `badge.json` earn it because Home
unmounts. Screens mount one at
a time (`Root`), so navigating anywhere takes both players down rather than
leaving them redrawing behind whatever is on top. They all carry most of the pause the
shine does: the gift box is still for two of its three seconds.

**Their loop lengths do not share a factor** — 102, 120, 156 and 180 frames. Four
marks on one screen that beat together read as a loading state; the whole point
is four separate things each worth pressing. Pick a new length against the ones
already there, not for its own sake.

`advert.json` is the loudest mark in the app, and deliberately: it is the only
control on Home that asks the player to _give_ something rather than offering
what they have earned. It runs one beat per two-second loop — crouch, hit, wake,
settle, sweep — with the screen squashing and kicking over, the head punching out
of it, two rings and four sparks leaving, and a highlight crossing the glass.

Two things learned building it, both general:

- **Subtlety is the wrong instinct at 36dp.** The first version had a two percent
  breathe and one small pop and read as a still image on a device. A mark this
  size gets a fraction of a second of peripheral attention; under about ten
  percent of its own width simply is not seen.
- **Sample only where a part is moving.** Sampling nine layers every frame across
  a whole loop put this file at 244KB, more than the win card's confetti, for a
  chip icon. `windowed` in the script emits keys inside each part's active window
  and holds flat outside; the same file is now 75KB and identical on screen.

`gleam.json` is `badge.json`'s treatment moved onto the primary buttons — Home's
Play, the win card's `Level N`, any dialog's confirm. It is a **separate, wider
file rather than the same one in a different box**, and that is the general
lesson: `resizeMode` fits a frame into what it is given, so a 100x100 composition
dropped into a 300x60 button is blown up three times and shows only its middle
fifth. Both of the badge's sparkles sit outside that strip. `gleam.json` is 300x64
with its sparkles spread along the length, which also survives the other
direction — in a 140dp dialog button `cover` scales by height and trims the ends,
costing a sparkle rather than the composition.

It is skipped on a `dim` face. A highlight travelling across a button that cannot
do its job says the opposite of what the dimming does. It is kept on an `on` face
— lit but not live, like "Equipped" — because that one is reporting a state worth
being pleased about.

## When Lottie is the wrong tool

`useMercury` — the highlight running along Home's progress fill — is Reanimated,
and it is the one mark on that card that is not a generated file. The reason is
worth knowing before reaching for Lottie again: **`resizeMode` fits a composition
into a box, and a progress fill has no box.** It is 4% wide on level 2 and 96%
wide on level 49. `cover` crops the sweep's travel away on a narrow fill;
`contain` squashes a 6dp band into a sliver. A Lottie needs to know its aspect.

A translating view does not — it is measured against whatever the fill turns out
to be, every frame, for free. Anything whose size is decided at runtime belongs in
Reanimated; anything in a fixed box can be a file.

## Two rules the format keeps catching people on

**`play(0)` is not "play from the start" on Android.** The JS layer defaults the
second argument to `-1`, and the Android view manager only takes the restart path
when both frames are given — otherwise it calls `resumeAnimation`, which picks up
wherever the player already was. A burst that has run once then does nothing on
every later press. iOS restarts either way, which is what makes it look like a
rendering bug on one platform instead of an argument bug on both. Pass a real end
frame; `useTapBurst` reads it from the composition's own `op`.

**Match the box to the frame's aspect.** `resizeMode="contain"` fits the whole
composition into whatever it is given, empty air included. `brew.json` shipped
18dp tall this way, and it is the first thing to check when a mark renders as a
smudge.
